Thirst
THURST
v.
Old English þyrstan, from þurst (thirst). Renders the Hebrew tsāmē’, “to thirst,” and the Greek dipsaō, “to thirst, be thirsty,” used both of the body’s craving for water and of the soul’s deep longing for God, righteousness, and the living water of Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

To thirst is to feel the urgent inward dryness that craves to be slaked—at its first reference the body’s need for water, at its deepest the soul’s need for God Himself. The Psalms set the verb’s great register: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God? And again: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is. Christ at the Feast of Tabernacles stood and cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water; and the apostle adds, this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive. The promise is universal: whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; the gospel offer is universal: and the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely; and the consummation is universal: I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely. Thirst is therefore the saint’s blessed inward register: the longing that drives him to the Fountain, the dryness that craves the springs of living water, the panting after God which is itself the Spirit’s evidence that the soul has been awakened. Christ Himself thirsted on the cross—a bodily thirst and, beneath it, the deeper drying-up of the soul under the wrath that bought us the living water we now drink. Thirst recovered is the soul recovered; thirst maintained is the soul healthy; thirst quenched, in the consummation, is the soul at last home: they shall thirst no more, neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat. For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines THIRST as a painful sensation occasioned by the want of drink; figuratively, a vehement desire of anything; an eager longing.

expand to see more

THIRST, v.i. — 1. To feel a painful sensation of the throat or fauces for want of drink; to feel a desire for drink. 2. To have a vehement desire of any thing. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God (Psa 42:2).

THIRST, n. — 1. The sensation occasioned by the want of drink; eagerness for drink. 2. A vehement desire of anything; as, a thirst for praise, for fame, for knowledge.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 42:1-2 — "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God."

Matthew 5:6 — "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled."

John 7:37-38 — "...If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water."

Revelation 22:17 — "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Spiritual thirsting is corrupted by the over-irrigated soul of the contemporary believer, who quenches every inward dryness with lesser drinks (entertainment, social media, busyness, the addictive comforts) and never lets the deep thirst form—and by the Jeremianic broken-cistern corruption of preferring the cisterns we hew out for ourselves to the fountain of living waters.

expand to see more

The contemporary believer is rarely permitted to be spiritually thirsty. Every inward dryness, every felt emptiness, every quiet ache of the soul is met immediately by the nearest lesser drink: the scroll of the phone, the next show, the snack, the conversation that fills the silence, the busyness that fills the calendar. The very dryness that, if allowed to form, would drive the soul to the springs of living waters is quenched in advance by an over-irrigated life of small consolations. The result is a generation that knows it is not satisfied but cannot articulate the thirst, because every formation of thirst is interrupted before it reaches its proper depth. The cure is the willingness to be dry—to turn off the lesser fountains, to let the silence and emptiness form, to permit the soul to discover its actual thirst, and to bring that thirst to the Fountain who alone can slake it.

The Jeremianic indictment is the older and graver corruption: my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water. Two evils, the LORD names. The first is forsaking the Fountain; the second is the active labor of digging cisterns of our own—careers, comforts, achievements, idols of every shape—to hold what they can never hold. The cisterns leak; the labor is endless; the thirst persists; and the Fountain stands forsaken. The recovery is the double turn the gospel announces and the soul, by the Spirit, performs: away from the broken cisterns, back to the Fountain. If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink—the offer is wide enough for every weary digger of broken cisterns and tender enough for every secret thirst no other water has slaked.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsāmē’ (to thirst) and Greek dipsaō (to thirst)—the soul’s deep longing for God set against the broken cisterns of Jeremiah 2 and answered by the living water of John 4 and 7.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsāmē’ (H6770) — to thirst, to be thirsty.

Hebrew tsāmā’ (H6772) — thirst (the noun).

Greek dipsaō (G1372) — to thirst (Matt 5:6; John 4:13-15; 7:37; 19:28; Rev 21:6; 22:17).

Greek dipsos (G1373) — thirst (the noun, 2 Cor 11:27).

Usage

"As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God—thirst is the saint’s blessed inward register."

"The over-irrigated soul of the contemporary believer never permits the deep thirst to form; recovery requires the willingness to be dry long enough for the proper craving to surface."

"Two evils, says Jeremiah: forsaking the Fountain, and digging our own broken cisterns—the Fountain still stands, the offer is still wide, if any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."
